paras: The lynching of Sam McIntyre was the killing of a Black man held on a murder charge, who was taken from the county jail at Forrest City, Arkansas, by a masked mob and hanged to a telegraph pole on or about April 23, 1919. The reports said the mob acted out of anger that his lawyers had won a postponement of his trial. The National Association for the Advancement of Colored People protested to Governor Charles H. Brough, calling it the twenty-first known lynching since the armistice, and its telegram made the case a news item across the Black press.

McIntyre was in the county jail at Forrest City charged with murdering a farmer. The Chicago Defender named the dead man as John Johnson, while the Associated Negro Press described him as "a Negro farmer" and the NAACP telegram as "another negro." His lawyers had obtained a postponement of his trial.

According to the Associated Negro Press dispatch, McIntire was "taken from the county jail by a masked mob and hanged to a telegraph pole." The Defender's version, badly garbled in print, adds that someone was "lured to the door by two prisoners" and quickly overpowered, but does not make clear who. Both dispatches attributed the lynching, with the hedges "it is said" and "it is supposed," to indignation over the postponed trial. None of the reports identified any member of the mob or gave its size or race.

On April 25 the NAACP, through its secretary John R. Shillady, telegraphed Governor Brough that press dispatches of April 23 told of McIntyre's lynching by a masked mob. Speaking for an association it said had 203 branches and 52,000 members, the telegram urged a thorough investigation and punishment of the mob, whose members, it said, had "declared that laws of the State of Arkansas are unworthy of regard." The NAACP noted that all twenty-one lynchings since the signing of the armistice had occurred in Southern states and said vigorous prosecution would "show America that Arkansas does not stand for mob violence." No report of an inquest, arrests, or a reply from the governor appears in the coverage.

The case reached Black readers by two routes. The NAACP's release, dated in New York on April 30 or May 1, ran on May 2 and 3 on the front pages of the St. Louis Argus under "Twenty-One Lynchings, All in South; Since Armistice," the Omaha Monitor under "Urges Punishment of Lynchers," and the Cleveland Advocate, and in a garbled form in the Baltimore Afro-American. The Ohio State Monitor printed the fullest version on May 10, including the text of the telegram itself.

A short Associated Negro Press dispatch from Forest City traveled separately and later, carrying datelines from May 1 to May 14. The Chicago Defender ran it on May 3 under "Man Who Killed Farmer Lynched by Angry Mobs," a heading that treated the murder charge as settled, buried within an unrelated column of news. The Phoenix Tribune headed the same text "Arkansas Justice" on May 17, and the Wisconsin Weekly Blade reprinted it on May 29 in its "Tabloid of News" beside an account of a lynching at Vicksburg. Where the NAACP framed the killing as a challenge to the rule of law and a count of Southern lynchings, the wire item reported it in two plain sentences.

The Black Dispatch printed the dispatch under "More Mob Violence" in a garbled form that named the victim "Sam McCullin" and said he "and his wife were killed in county jail," the only report of a second victim. Its wording otherwise follows the ANP dispatch, and every other report names a single man, McIntyre or McIntire. The later datelines and the phrase "last night" in the wire item conflict with the April 23 date, but the NAACP telegram, dated April 25 and citing dispatches of April 23, is the earliest dated evidence.

reader.title: Lynching of Sam McIntyre
bases: Every report describes a Black man accused of murder who was taken from the county jail at Forrest City by a masked mob and hanged (A1, A7, A8).

McIntyre was taken from the county jail by a 'masked mob' and hanged to a telegraph pole while awaiting trial on a murder charge (A7, A8), and the reports ascribe the killing to anger at the postponement of that trial (A3, A8), a killing outside the law by a group acting on a pretext of justice.

The NAACP's telegram, based on press dispatches of April 23 (A7), and a separate Associated Negro Press dispatch (A8, A9) agree on the core event, a Black prisoner at Forrest City taken from jail by a masked mob and lynched; the Defender (A3) carries a version of the same dispatch text.

accounts.label: NAACP telegram and release
accounts.gist: Citing press dispatches of April 23, the NAACP said Sam McIntyre was lynched by a masked mob at Forrest City over indignation at the postponement of his trial for murdering another Black man, and demanded investigation and punishment.

accounts.label: Associated Negro Press dispatch
accounts.gist: Sam McIntire was taken from the county jail by a masked mob and hanged to a telegraph pole; he was charged with murdering a Negro farmer, and 'it is said' the lynching followed his lawyers' obtaining a postponement of his trial.

accounts.label: Chicago Defender brief
accounts.gist: A garbled version of the same dispatch names the dead farmer as John Johnson and mentions someone 'lured to the door by two prisoners' before being overpowered.

accounts.label: Black Dispatch (ANP, garbled)
accounts.gist: Names the victim 'Sam McCullin' and says he and his wife were killed in the county jail by a mob and hanged to a telegraph pole.

framing.detail: The NAACP release, run as front-page news under headlines such as 'Twenty-One Lynchings, All in South; Since Armistice' and 'Urges Punishment of Lynchers', placed the killing in a count of post-armistice lynchings and said the mob had declared Arkansas law 'unworthy of regard'.
The Phoenix Tribune headed the ANP dispatch 'Arkansas Justice', an ironic heading over a plain wire account.
The Defender's heading 'Man Who Killed Farmer Lynched by Angry Mobs' stated the murder accusation as fact; the Black Dispatch ran its brief as 'More Mob Violence'.

conflicts.note: All forms appear to name one man; 'McCullin' occurs only in a badly garbled Black Dispatch brief whose wording otherwise matches the ANP dispatch.
Only the Black Dispatch mentions a wife; its sentence is internally garbled ('were killed ... and was hanged') and the same ANP text elsewhere names one victim.
The NAACP telegram, dated April 25 and citing dispatches of April 23, is the earliest dated evidence; the later datelines look like datelines added when the ANP item was reprinted.
Compatible versions; only the Defender gives a name.
